I had thought of that myself. Apocalypse Now had a good deal of superimposition in a couple of sequences: early on, Willard has a dilirum scene that's done almost entirely in superimposition, and then there's that the trekking montage just before they reach Kurtz' compound, that's also very rich in superimposition, mostly of that ominous Indu idol, which is of course repeated in the film's closing.

The Fellowship of the Ring sometimes used superimposition: there's a good deal of it in the prolouge, especially the tail-end of the prologue, where Jackson was clearly trying to channel something of Terrence Malick. Also later on when Frodo is taken to Rivendell.

Actually, writing it out it strikes me: many of these examples are delirium scenes, which goes into your point about it supposedly breaking "the audience’s suspension of disbelief." Along with split-screen (also used by Gance) its just percieved as a less naturalistic form of filmmaking.

>If you know any modern films which use superimposition in an interesting way please let me know

Annette uses lot of superimpositions. I think that has to do with Carax’s obsession with silent cinema, which is one of the appeals of his films for me. He meshes the silent cinema techniques and feel with more modern sensibility.

This comes from the aesthetic movement called "French Impressionist Cinema" in the 1920s, with Gance, as you noted, but also Epstein, Germaine Dulac or early Jean Renoir.

I believe there is also superimposition in Eisenstein's Octobre (for instance), where the figures of the revolution are superimposed with the animals that represent them.

I agree with you it's not used nearly as often as it should (except to induce dreamlike atmosphere or something...). Like the "Iris effect" used a lot in the silent era and not anymore nowadays...

Thinking myself in the directors position I feel it would be something that draws too much attention to itself, takes the people out of the movie.


I think what happens is that you people choose to either do a film with a lot of unusual techniques where you will propably also find superimposition or a very "clean" movie where you do without any such technique.


Thus, its not just superimposition you will also not find e.g. black and white in flashbacks or overexposure or timelapse. I feel the modern filmmaker would actually see themselves as "disciplined" in a way were they consciously deny themselves such tricks even when they feel drawn to do it.


They consider such stuff as somehow self indulgent or something that a hobbyist would do, not a professional. 


Its a bit like what people would associate with the "zen" term. The true artist is someone who denies any kind of superficial ornamentation or meandering, very stripped down and to the point, and always with that visual clarity that is antithetical to e.g superimposition.

It's fallen out of style, and it's evolved. Now, it's used for cell phones and other technology. "The Killer" features just one such superimposition (IIRC) and it's pretty jarring. 

Editing, now that it's digital, is much much much much easier. Everything is easier. 

Superimpositions might have also been more popular back when they were *hard* to do, and expensive. To show off, maybe a little. 

Also, back then, there were few such tools in the toolbox. Superimpositions were one of a handful of tools. Now there are infinite tools with technology.
I would rather watch 1,000 movies where there are inexplicably no cell phones post-2007-ish than a single one with that jarring phone overlay.

Hasn't this just become green screen?  It's as if they used it as a means to an end without thinking of the actual stylization of said means.  It's something interesting I've never considered and will be doing so moving forward.  Thanks for the post!
Great insight.

I'm reminded of Speed Racer. Not quite superimposition in the classic way, but it makes extensive use of spatial (as opposed to temporal) juxtaposition of shots

It's frankly incredibly striking, and I want to see much more of it. Sure, not a lot of mainstream movies use it, for the reasons cited in other comments, but if you're making an indie arthouse piece, there are just so many things you can do with a camera that people don't even try to explore

I know there are plenty of experimental films like My Winnipeg or Color of Pomegranates that do truly wild compositions, but the space still feels underexplored in general. I mean, Speed Racer is in many ways a not-very-good movie, but its so much more beloved than it could have been because it dared to imagine a *truly* unique style of editing
I haven’t seen a single Carax film even though he’s been on my radar for a long time. This comment could be the final push I need to dive into his filmography!

Apocalypse Now and The Fellowship of the Ring were the two modern examples I had in mind! I was lucky enough to catch the entire LOTR trilogy in theaters a couple of weeks ago and it struck me how often Peter Jackson uses superimposition and dissolves.
Nice, but bear in mind that Annette and Pola X are his most divisive films so not the best starting points.

Yeah, I guess it’s true that green screen has replaced the special effects aspect of superimposition. I hadn’t thought of that. An important distinction though is that green screen hides the fact that what looks like a single shot consists of multiple different shots, whereas in Gance’s Napoleon, for example, that is the point.

One of my favourites in this respect is Panos Cosmatos' hallucinatory debut film Beyond the ***Black Rainbow*** (2010). It's part of the general dreamy feel of the movie, and in combination with the music has a very strong effect of dream/hallucination.

I think it's also present quite a lot in the same director's ***Mandy*** (2018), most notably in a shot which superimposes the faces of a woman and the man who's taunting her and has dosed her with LSD. 

Seem to remember it in Denis Wheatley's films ***A Field in England*** (2013) and **On the Earth** (2021), both films with a strong hallucinatory feel. 

I think both Cosmatos and Wheatley are channeling the Jodorowsky alchemical-shamanistic aesthetic of The Holy Mountain (1973) and others.

I tend to associate the superimposition montage with the 30s and 40s (printing presses, spinning newspapers) but you can find examples of it through the New Hollywood era. Past that it seems to have been overtaken by the iconic 80s Montage of Rocky sequels and the like.

Agreed which is something that is probably getting lost in all the tech and low cost solutions we have.  This is the type of thing that's nice to ponder on while considering the composition of a shot.  In fact if you took the value added creatively from superimposing something and focused on that with modern solutions one could potentially scale up the impact of said technique.  Like imagine shooting something on a green screen with the intent of using it to stand out with a multi-layered/masked approach to the post production.  All interesting stuff that could easily slip through the cracks.

There was a post just recently concerning the fading of dissolves in movies. To me the decline of these techniques (and the prominence of others like long takes) suggests a trend away from filmmakers using a genuinely cinematic form, toward just "this shot" and not "this shot *and this shot*" via the use of montage, superimposition, etc.

(I think it's not for nothing that this coincides with the static and stagey *Jeanne Dielman* taking the place of 'greatest film' in critics' opinion.)
I think the animal impositions is in his film Strike not October.
Thanks. I wasn't sure which one, and picked the wrong one obviously...

Superimposition particularly flourished in the 1970s when video became available; that technology made it much easier for filmmakers to experiment. Godard’s *Numero Deux* is one of the textbook examples of the technique.

This is an incredibly experimental example, but the film Sleep Has Her House by Scott Barley has some of the most incredible superimpositions I have seen. Completely modifies the feeling of the shots into this sort of arboreal waterfall shone through by roving god-rays. I also really love the superimposition in one of the later episodes of Twin Peaks: The Return where Coop is just staring out at the viewer while all the spoilery stuff happens in the TP sheriff's office before that shivery statement: "We live inside a dream." Beautifully metaphysical.

Surprised to hear this about Pola X. Like many fans of Scott Walker, I discovered Carax through that film because Scott Walker provided its soundtrack. Having seen all of Carax’s work multiple times now, I still rate it highly.
